title: “Your mother was raped by a dog”: the absurdity paradox
subtitle: An insult so absurd that nobody could believe it. The absurdity is a strong answer to a libel claim and, by itself, no defence to a criminal charge. Disclaimers do not change either answer.
summary: Defamation is hard to predict for a simple reason. Words are judged through a hypothetical reasonable reader, the writer’s intention is irrelevant, and since 2014 that reader is imagined by a judge, not a jury. Take a specimen insult, “You are so ugly because your mother was raped by a dog”, sent as a private message. As libel it fails three times over: a message sent only to the person it insults is not published to anyone else; no reasonable reader takes it as a statement of fact, which is what the courts call “mere vulgar abuse”; and nobody’s reputation suffers serious harm. As a crime it does not need to be believed. Section 127 asks whether it was grossly offensive or indecent and sent over a public network. The Malicious Communications Act asks whether it was sent to cause distress. In 2026 a councillor argued that “you cannot melt people down”. He was convicted. Adding disclaimers (“I’m not accusing, I’m only asking, hypothetically”) does not help either way: the courts read the whole message, and the sender’s intention is irrelevant to what it means.
scope: England and Wales. The specimen sentence is ours, written to test the law and aimed at no real person. We quote it in order to analyse it, which is the kind of context the courts say changes what words are.
status_note: Our analysis of how the cited statutes and judgments apply to an invented sentence, read from the official texts on 11 November 2026. The reasonable-reader section was checked against the National Archives texts of Jeynes, Stocker and Rufus on 12 November 2026, and the House of Lords text of DPP v Collins was checked the same day. No court has ruled on this sentence, and whether words are grossly offensive or indecent is a question of fact for the court in each case. This is legal research, not legal advice.

sections.title: The specimen
sections.intro: One sentence, sent as a direct message to one person.

paragraphs.text: “You are so ugly because your mother was raped by a dog.”

It does three things at once. It insults the recipient. It makes a claim about a third person, the mother, involving sexual violence and an animal. And it is absurd as a statement of fact: nobody reading it would think it was reporting something that happened.

The absurdity sits in the word “because”: a dog cannot father a human child. The law assumes its hypothetical reader knows that. It does not ask whether every real reader does, and it hears no evidence from real readers about what they understood.

We wrote it because it separates two areas of law that are often confused. Civil defamation protects reputation, so it cares what a reasonable reader would take the words to mean. The criminal communications offences protect other things, so they mostly do not.

sections.title: Why it fails as libel
sections.intro: Libel is a claim brought by the person defamed, at their own cost. It has three hurdles this sentence cannot clear.

entries.title: Hurdle one: nobody else read it

paragraphs.text: “At common law, a cause of action for libel is made out by proof that the defendant was responsible for the publication to one or more third parties of a written statement that bore a defamatory meaning about the claimant.”
A direct message read only by the person it insults has not been published to a third party. If the sender posts it publicly, or into a group, this hurdle disappears. The next two remain.

Courts read words the way an ordinary reader would. Some remarks, in their context, are obviously “not to be taken literally or seriously” and are understood as abuse. Mr Justice Eady called this “mere vulgar abuse”, an old idea from slander cases, and treated it as part of working out what words mean rather than as a separate defence.
He said online exchanges are often like casual conversation in a bar: “uninhibited, casual and ill thought out”, with readers who expect “a certain amount of repartee or ‘give and take’”.
Nobody reads the specimen as a report of fact about anyone’s mother. That is why it reads as abuse.
Since 2014 a statement is not defamatory unless its publication has caused, or is likely to cause, serious harm to the claimant’s reputation.

That harm is measured in the minds of readers, not by how hurt the claimant feels. It “is the effect of a publication in the mind of a third-party publishee (reader)”, and is “not constituted by a claimant’s own subjective reaction”.
An insult nobody believes changes nobody’s opinion of anyone. And the factual part of the sentence is about the mother, not the recipient, so if anyone had a claim at all it would be hers.

sections.title: Why it can still be a crime
sections.intro: The criminal offences do not ask whether anyone believed it. They ask what was sent, how, and why.

entries.title: Section 127: sent over a public network
entries.kind: Statute and House of Lords judgment, applied by us

paragraphs.text: Sending a message that is “grossly offensive or of an indecent, obscene or menacing character” over a public electronic communications network is an offence. Ordinary messaging apps run over the internet, which counts, though the network element still has to be shown for the message in question.

The question is whether the words are “liable to cause gross offence to those to whom it relates”, judged by reasonably enlightened contemporary standards in context. It does not matter whether the message is believed, or even read.

In our view, a sentence built on the rape of the recipient’s mother by an animal is a strong candidate for both “indecent” and “grossly offensive”. That is a question of fact for magistrates, and a court could take a different view of a single crude insult.

entries.title: The Malicious Communications Act: sent to hurt

paragraphs.text: The 1988 Act punishes sending another person a message that is indecent or grossly offensive, where one purpose of sending it is to cause that person distress or anxiety. The maximum is two years’ imprisonment.

Sent directly to its target, an insult like this invites the inference that one purpose was to cause distress. That purpose must still be proved in context; the words alone do not settle it. Where it is proved, this offence fits the specimen better than section 127 does.

entries.title: The absurdity defence, tried in court
entries.kind: Press reporting of a magistrates’ court verdict · appeal intended

paragraphs.text: Glenn Gibbins posted that Nigerians in Sunderland should be melted down to fill potholes. In court he said: “It’s an unreal scenario, you cannot melt people down, anyone that takes that literally… you cannot do that.” On 9 November 2026 he was convicted. His lawyers said he would appeal.

His post was about a group, our specimen is about one person, but the argument is the same: that a literally impossible scenario cannot be taken seriously. In defamation that argument usually wins, depending on the whole publication. In a communications prosecution the court looks instead at what the words say about the people they target.

It is unlikely to be obscene in the sense of the Obscene Publications Act 1959, which asks whether material tends to “deprave and corrupt” the people likely to read it. A crude insult is not that kind of material.

It contains no threat of death or serious harm, so the Online Safety Act threatening-communications offence does not apply. Sent once, it is not harassment, which needs a course of conduct, meaning conduct on at least two occasions.
Add a threat, a second message and a few other ingredients, and the count rises quickly. That is Message ultra.

sections.title: The disclaimer paradox
sections.intro: Now add disclaimers. “I am not accusing you. I am not implying anything. I am not suggesting anything. I am only asking, purely hypothetically.” The more of them there are, the more a reasonable reader asks why they are needed.

paragraphs.text: The absurd version: “I am not accusing anyone of anything. I am not implying anything, and I am not suggesting anything. This is purely hypothetical, and I am only asking: is it possible that your mother was raped by a dog?”

A plausible version, with the allegation described rather than written: “I’m not accusing [a named neighbour] of anything, and I’m not implying anything. I’m only asking, purely hypothetically, why [the neighbour] was seen near [the place where a crime was committed] that night.”
The two pull apart. The first stays absurd however it is phrased. In the second, the disclaimers are all that stand between a question and an accusation.

entries.title: A question can be an accusation
entries.citation: The Lord McAlpine of West Green v Bercow [2013] EWHC 1342 (QB)

paragraphs.text: “The law is clear that words may be defamatory in whatever form they are used. A question, or a rhetorical question, or any other form of words may, in principle, be understood to convey a defamatory meaning.”

Sally Bercow tweeted “Why is Lord McAlpine trending? *Innocent face*”. The judge held that it meant he was a paedophile who had sexually abused boys in care, which was false. “Innocent face” was her disclaimer, and those two words decided the meaning:

“the reasonable reader would understand the words ‘innocent face’ as being insincere and ironical. There is no sensible reason for including those words in the Tweet if they are to be taken as meaning that the Defendant simply wants to know the answer to a factual question.”

In Stocker v Stocker the Supreme Court restated the test for meaning, quoting the Court of Appeal in Jeynes. Two of its rules settle the disclaimer question: “The intention of the publisher is irrelevant.” And: “The article must be read as a whole, and any ‘bane and antidote’ taken together.”

A disclaimer is offered as the antidote. It works when, read with everything else, it really changes what a reasonable reader takes from the words. It fails when the reader sees it as a device: a denial of the very thing the words point at. What the writer says they meant does not decide it.

entries.title: Why more disclaimers can make it worse

paragraphs.text: The reasonable reader asks why each disclaimer is there. One honest qualification can be taken at face value. A stack of them, each denying an accusation nobody has made yet, invites the question the McAlpine judge asked of “innocent face”: what sensible reason is there for including them, unless the writer means the opposite? The more the writer insists the question is only hypothetical, the more the reader wonders who it is about.

That is our reading, not a rule of law. Courts do not count disclaimers, and a disclaimer does not always backfire. The test is still what the whole publication conveys to a reader who is neither naïve nor avid for scandal. A hypothetical about no one accuses no one. A hypothetical that points at a real person, at a moment when readers are asking about him, points the finger.

For the absurd specimen the disclaimers change nothing. As libel it was never a statement of fact, so there is nothing for them to cancel. For the criminal offences, “purely hypothetical” does not alter whether a message about someone’s mother, sent to them, is indecent or grossly offensive, or why it was sent. A disclaimer is part of the context, but it cannot turn the message into something else.

So the paradox runs both ways. Disclaimers cannot make the absurd believable, and they cannot make a believable insinuation innocent. We apply this to ourselves: on live-case pages we do not set uncharged material next to a defendant’s name and add that its meaning should not be assumed, because a disclaimer does not change what a reader takes from the juxtaposition.

sections.title: The hypothetical reasonable reader: a person who does not exist, interpreting meanings that may never have been intended
sections.intro: The law of defamation decides meaning through a person who is not called to give evidence. That reader may read between the lines and indulge in a certain amount of loose thinking, but must not be avid for scandal. The criteria below are a defamation-law framework. They do not automatically supply the test for a criminal speech offence.

entries.title: The reasonable reader's playbook
entries.kind: Supreme Court judgment, quoting the Court of Appeal

table.caption: The eight criteria from Jeynes, paragraph 14, as set out by Lord Kerr in Stocker, paragraph 35, for a unanimous court
columns: The test, as quoted in Stocker
rows: The governing principle is reasonableness.

The hypothetical reasonable reader is not naïve, but he is not unduly suspicious. He can read between the lines. He can read in an implication more readily than a lawyer and may indulge in a certain amount of loose thinking, but he must be treated as being a man who is not avid for scandal and someone who does not, and should not, select one bad meaning where other non-defamatory meanings are available.
Over-elaborate analysis is best avoided.
The intention of the publisher is irrelevant.
The article must be read as a whole, and any ‘bane and antidote’ taken together.
The hypothetical reader is taken to be representative of those who would read the publication in question.

In delimiting the range of permissible defamatory meanings, the court should rule out any meaning which, ‘can only emerge as the produce of some strained, or forced, or utterly unreasonable interpretation …’
It follows that ‘it is not enough to say that by some person or another the words might be understood in a defamatory sense.’

paragraphs.text: Lord Kerr, with whom the rest of the court agreed, treated the choice of a single meaning as well entrenched. Guidance as to how the judge should set about that task had been given by Sir Anthony Clarke MR in Jeynes. The table quotes the eight criteria as they appear in Stocker, paragraph 35. We have omitted only the case citations that follow the quoted words in criteria (7) and (8). The original wording in Jeynes, paragraph 14, is to the same effect; the differences are two commas in criterion (2) and the form of those citations.

table.caption: Our questions about the eight criteria, not a further legal test

Who determines what is reasonable?

Where does healthy inference become excessive suspicion?
Avoid over-analysis

paragraphs.text: Each criterion answers one question and leaves another open. These are our questions, not a ninth legal test, and not implications that any court has drawn as a list.

entries.title: The Rufus rider: “should not select one bad meaning” describes the reader
entries.kind: Court of Appeal and Supreme Court judgments

paragraphs.text: Sharp LJ added a rider to the second criterion in Rufus v Elliott. Lord Kerr quoted it:

To this I would only add that the words ‘should not select one bad meaning where other non-defamatory meanings are available’ are apt to be misleading without fuller explanation. They obviously do not mean in a case such as this one, where it is open to a defendant to contend either on a capability application or indeed at trial that the words complained of are not defamatory of the claimant, that the tribunal adjudicating on the question must then select the non-defamatory meaning for which the defendant contends. Instead, those words are ‘part of the description of the hypothetical reasonable reader, rather than (as) a prescription of how such a reader should attribute meanings to words complained of as defamatory’: see McAlpine v Bercow [2013] EWHC 1342 (QB), paras 63 to 66.

So, Lord Kerr said, where a range of meanings is available and one of them is not defamatory, “the court is not obliged to select the non-defamatory meaning”. The touchstone remains what the ordinary reasonable reader would consider the words to mean. A theoretically possible innocent reading does not compel that result.

That is the reading Tugendhat J had already given the same words in McAlpine. He treated them as a description of the reader, not as a rule that the less derogatory meaning must be chosen. It would be unreasonable always to adopt a bad meaning where a non-defamatory meaning was available. It would also be naïve always to adopt the less derogatory meaning. Bercow was held liable on the meaning the judge found.

table.caption: The single-meaning rule as a legal device, not a claim about what every reader thought
rows: Actual readers may take different interpretations
The court still settles on a single meaning
The reasonable reader is a legal construct
No real reader gives evidence of what the words meant to them

paragraphs.text: Whether the analogy between a single defamatory meaning and a sole meaning to be given to a contractual term, statutory provision or notice is apt (which I take leave to doubt), it is clear that the single meaning approach is well entrenched in the law of defamation and neither party in the present appeal sought to impeach it. And, whatever else may be said of it, it provides a practical, workable solution. Where a statement has more than one plausible meaning, the question of whether defamation has occurred can only be answered by deciding that one particular meaning should be ascribed to the statement.

The judge is not claiming that everyone actually understood the publication identically. The rule supplies a workable legal answer to an inherently variable linguistic problem. Since 2014 that choice is almost always made by a judge, sitting without a jury.

entries.title: A disclaimer does not dictate the meaning

paragraphs.text: The same tension is at work in the disclaimed specimens above, and in a plainer form of words: “I am not suggesting that the decision-maker committed fraud. There is no evidence of fraud. This is merely a hypothetical question about whether fraud might be investigated.”

A reasonable reader might take that as a genuine clarification excluding an allegation; as an expression of uncertainty about potential wrongdoing; or as an insinuation dressed as a disclaimer. But the reader is not entitled to choose the most scandalous interpretation merely because it is possible. Equally, the publisher cannot dictate the meaning by declaring that no accusation is intended. That is the tension between criteria (2), (4) and (5).

table.caption: Names used in the National Archives text of Stocker, including passages that quote other judgments. Counted on 12 November 2026, as exact phrases
columns: What the word stresses, on our reading
rows: ordinary reasonable reader
The full label: ordinary, and reasonable
ordinary reader
Not a lawyer. The court must “step aside from a lawyerly analysis”
hypothetical reasonable reader
The reader is imagined, so no real reader gives evidence
hypothetical reader
The same imagined figure, in Jeynes criterion (6)
typical reader
Stands for the actual audience: “the typical reader of a Facebook post”

paragraphs.text: Stocker switches between these names without marking any difference, so they are best read as synonyms for one figure. Each word stresses a different side of it. “Hypothetical” marks that the reader is imagined, and that no real reader gives evidence of meaning. “Reasonable” is the character in Jeynes criteria (1) and (2): not naïve, not unduly suspicious. “Ordinary” is the instruction not to parse the words as a lawyer would. “Typical” points to the actual audience in criterion (6), which is why “the typical reader of a Facebook post” is not the reader of a law report. Lord Kerr once makes the equation express: “a typical (ie an ordinary reasonable) reader”. That wording is not an extra hit for the exact phrase “typical reader”.

Section 127 uses none of these names. Lord Carswell described the magistrates’ task as deciding whether a message was grossly offensive “in the eyes of reasonable people” (para 18). In paragraph 22 he referred to “reasonable members of society in general” and “reasonable citizens”. These are different names for a different imagined person, whose job is to decide whether a message is grossly offensive, not what it means as a matter of defamation.

entries.title: A defamation framework, not a criminal one

paragraphs.text: There is one further limit. The Jeynes criteria, the single-meaning rule and the Rufus rider belong to the law of defamation. They cannot automatically be transplanted into criminal speech offences, whose statutory elements and tests differ. Section 127, as the next section sets out, asks a different question of a different imagined person. The absurdity paradox in this chapter depends on that difference.

sections.title: The paradox in one table
sections.intro: The same words, judged by two different questions.

paragraphs.text: Libel asks what the words did to someone’s reputation. The communications offences ask what the sender did with a public network, or with another person’s peace of mind.

Both areas of law rely on an imagined reasonable person. In defamation that person is a reader deciding what words mean, and absurdity helps them. In section 127 that person applies “reasonably enlightened, but not perfectionist, contemporary standards” to decide what is grossly offensive, which is a judgment about taste. Lord Bingham accepted that these standards change over time. The result is an offence whose limits are set case by case, by magistrates, after the message has been sent.

Who imagines the reader? Since 1 January 2014 defamation trials have been heard without a jury unless the court orders otherwise, so in practice a judge decides what words mean, often as a preliminary issue before anything else is tried. That is how McAlpine was decided. No real reader gives evidence, and the writer’s intention is irrelevant: the meaning is the one the judge attributes to an imagined fair-minded reader.

entries.kind: House of Lords and High Court judgments, compared by us

paragraphs.text: Defamation and section 127 each rely on an imagined person, but not the same one. The defamation reader decides what words mean. The section 127 standard decides whether a message is grossly offensive. They were built by different courts for different jobs, and no judgment we have found says how they fit together.

“There can be no yardstick of gross offensiveness otherwise than by the application of reasonably enlightened, but not perfectionist, contemporary standards to the particular message sent in its particular context.”

The section 127 standard belongs to society, not to the audience. Lord Carswell thought the justices may have “placed some weight on the reaction of the actual listeners to the messages, rather than considering the reactions of reasonable members of society in general”. The defamation reader is the reverse: a reasonable representative of the people who actually read the words, in McAlpine the “users of Twitter who follow the Defendant”.

Not obviously. Before magistrates can ask whether a message is grossly offensive, someone has to decide what it means, and Collins does not say whose reading fixes that. It does not import the defamation reader, and the defamation cases do not mention reasonable enlightenment. In practice the same magistrates decide both questions, from the standpoint of society in general.

The gap is where the absurdity paradox lives. The defamation reader, who is not avid for scandal, reads the specimen as abuse and stops there. The reasonably enlightened standard asks a different question of the same words, whether they are liable to cause gross offence to those to whom they relate, and the absurdity does not answer it. Both imagined people are designed to resist over-sensitivity, one against finding scandal and one against perfectionism, yet they can reach opposite results on one sentence.

entries.title: Can you change the law by changing the standards?

paragraphs.text: “The reasonable man adapts himself to the world: the unreasonable one persists in trying to adapt the world to himself. Therefore all progress depends on the unreasonable man.”
Our version, from the artwork at the end of this section: reasonable on old terms is unreasonable; unreasonable is reasonable.

Partly, yes. Where the law is written as a standard rather than a rule, it moves when society moves, without Parliament changing a word. Lord Bingham accepted that “usages and sensitivities may change over time”, and that language once insulting can become “a badge of honour”. Lord Carswell described magistrates as people “expected to apply the standards of today’s society”. Dishonesty works the same way: since Ivey, it is judged by “the (objective) standards of ordinary decent people”.

The limits. You cannot set the standard yourself: it belongs to reasonable members of society in general, and your standards count only once enough people share them that a court treats them as ordinary. That is changed by argument, publishing and persuasion, slowly and together. Standards can also tighten as well as loosen. And only standards move this way: definitions, maximum sentences and lists of what may be reported change only through Parliament or the higher courts.

So the law’s reasonable person is a conformist by design, and Shaw’s unreasonable person is the one who changes what the conformist accepts. Blasphemy shows the whole cycle: it fell out of use as public standards moved, and Parliament abolished it in 2008, recognising a change that had already happened. To be “unreasonably reasonable” is to act on tomorrow’s standard while being judged by today’s.
